Seven published analyses

Benjamin E. Bagozzi

Source: vignettes/applications.Rmd
applications.Rmd

The package ships seven datasets taken from the replication archives of published studies, released by their authors under CC0 at the Harvard Dataverse; two of them are extracts of British Election Study surveys, which the UK Data Service distributes under CC BY 4.0 and their help pages cite. Four reproduce their published models (Liou, Liu et al., Glasgow, and the penalized fits of Cook, Niehaus and Zuhlke) and one equals the authors’ own estimator on the same data (Baeck, Debus and Imre), and the package’s tests check that they do; the other two illustrate varying choice sets and rankings. This vignette uses each to show a part of the package: a clustered multinomial logit with interactions, an experiment with a “don’t know” answer, the IIA tests on the classic British election data, separation and Firth’s penalized likelihood, varying choice sets and rankings with ties, unlabelled alternatives, and a rank-ordered logit with its stability test.

Sanctions, force, and domestic unrest

sanctions holds the country-years of Liou (2024): does a government facing mass protest at home turn to economic sanctions abroad, and does a strong legislative opposition make that more likely? The outcome has three alternatives, no coercion (the base), sanctions, and military force, and the hypothesis is an interaction of a nonviolent campaign with the opposition’s seat share. The published Table 1, with standard errors clustered by country, reproduces (its log-likelihood is -1161.5576).

data(sanctions)
table(sanctions$outcome)
#> 
#>      none sanctions     force 
#>      2400       169       416
ms <- mnl(outcome ~ nonviolent * opposition + violent * opposition + growth + inflation +
            leg_election + exec_election + gdppc + trade + milex + democracy + human_rights +
            coldwar + peaceyears + I(peaceyears^2) + I(peaceyears^3),
          data = sanctions, cluster = sanctions$ccode, se = "cluster")
ms$loglik
#> [1] -1161.558
summary(ms)$coefficients[c("sanctions:nonviolent", "sanctions:opposition", "sanctions:nonviolent:opposition"), ]
#>                                  Estimate Std. Error   z value     Pr(>|z|)
#> sanctions:nonviolent            -1.527710   1.059604 -1.441774 0.1493661220
#> sanctions:opposition            -3.736708   1.134080 -3.294924 0.0009844841
#> sanctions:nonviolent:opposition  8.146855   2.926213  2.784095 0.0053677338

Stata’s clustered standard errors carry the small-sample factor G/(G−1)\sqrt{G/(G-1)}, here 137/136\sqrt{137/136}; the package’s are smaller by that factor and otherwise equal. An interaction is read through probabilities. Averaged over the country-years, the probability of sanctions with and without a nonviolent campaign, at an opposition share of 6 and of 49 percent (the paper’s one standard deviation below and above the mean):

avg <- function(nv, opp) colMeans(predict(ms, newdata = transform(sanctions, nonviolent = nv, opposition = opp)))
round(rbind(`no campaign, opposition 6%` = avg(0, 0.06), `campaign, opposition 6%` = avg(1, 0.06),
            `no campaign, opposition 49%` = avg(0, 0.49), `campaign, opposition 49%` = avg(1, 0.49)), 3)
#>                              none sanctions force
#> no campaign, opposition 6%  0.784     0.097 0.119
#> campaign, opposition 6%     0.823     0.051 0.126
#> no campaign, opposition 49% 0.810     0.034 0.155
#> campaign, opposition 49%    0.763     0.190 0.047

With a nonviolent campaign under way, the probability of sanctions rises from 0.05 to 0.19 as the opposition’s share goes from 6 to 49 percent (the paper reports 4.9 and 18.5 percent); without a campaign it falls.

Vaccination and “don’t know”

fluvax is the survey experiment of Liu et al. (2024): would respondents take a flu vaccine developed by the United States alone, with China, or with Japan? The answers are no, don’t know, and yes, and the experiment randomizes the partner. Table 3, Model 1 reproduces with robust standard errors.

data(fluvax)
mf <- mnl(vaccinate ~ condition + age + female + educ + income + race + party + knowledge,
          data = fluvax, se = "robust")
summary(mf)$coefficients[grep("condition|republican", names(coef(mf))), ]
#>                               Estimate Std. Error    z value     Pr(>|z|)
#> dont_know:conditionus_china -0.1209197  0.1839723 -0.6572709 5.110068e-01
#> dont_know:conditionus_japan  0.1556454  0.1934296  0.8046619 4.210148e-01
#> dont_know:partyrepublican   -0.6778291  0.1794010 -3.7782895 1.579093e-04
#> yes:conditionus_china       -0.3848484  0.1709685 -2.2509899 2.438617e-02
#> yes:conditionus_japan        0.3465168  0.1741942  1.9892559 4.667296e-02
#> yes:partyrepublican         -1.3213227  0.1668037 -7.9214224 2.348088e-15
first_difference(mf, "condition", from = "us_alone", to = "us_china")
#> First differences: condition from us_alone to us_china at the covariate profile (delta intervals at 95%)
#>  alternative  from    to   diff  lower  upper
#>           no 0.186 0.238  0.052  0.001  0.102
#>    dont_know 0.207 0.234  0.027 -0.028  0.083
#>          yes 0.607 0.528 -0.079 -0.151 -0.007

At the covariate profile, naming China as the partner lowers the probability of a yes by about eight points. A “don’t know” can mix the undecided with respondents who give it whatever is asked. The score test of the multinomial logit against captive choosers, computed from the multinomial logit fit alone, does not reject here, and neither does its likelihood-ratio form (a constant captive share of “don’t know” gains 0.41 in log-likelihood, p = 0.18). The inflated multinomial logit with “don’t know” as the inflated alternative improves the log-likelihood by 4.6 for four more parameters, which the information criteria read in opposite directions:

captivity_test(mf)
#> Score test of the multinomial logit against captive choosers (dogit; one-sided z per alternative, joint chi-square) 
#>                test statistic df p.value
#>         captive: no    -0.050 NA   0.520
#>  captive: dont_know     0.631 NA   0.264
#>        captive: yes    -0.062 NA   0.525
#>               joint     0.575  3   0.902
mi <- imnl(vaccinate ~ condition + age + female + educ + income + race + party + knowledge |
             age + educ + knowledge, data = fluvax, inflate = "dont_know")
compare_models(MNL = mf, inflated = mi)
#>     model
#>       MNL
#>  inflated
#>                                                                       type
#>                                                          Multinomial logit
#>  Inflated multinomial logit (inflated alternative: dont_know, logit split)
#>    inflate    n df    loglik      AIC      BIC mcfadden converged boundary
#>            1334 26 -1281.466 2614.931 2750.026    0.090      TRUE    FALSE
#>  dont_know 1334 30 -1276.870 2613.740 2769.618    0.093      TRUE    FALSE
#>  ill_conditioned n_modes
#>            FALSE       1
#>            FALSE       2

The inflated fit’s search found two distinct maxima (mi$n_modes, with a message), and the highest is reported; one more search ended where a split coefficient diverges, which mi$search lists as a boundary. The multinomial logit is the boundary of the inflated model, so boot_lr_test(mf, mi) gives the calibrated comparison (not run here: every replicate refits the inflated model).

Issue distances in Britain, 1987

bes1987 holds the 1987 British General Election Study respondents of Glasgow (2001), with the distance between each voter and each party on seven issues: the classic example of the debate about the independence of irrelevant alternatives in multiparty elections. The multinomial logit of the paper’s Appendix A reproduces (log-likelihood -1477.56).

data(bes1987)
fb <- chosen ~ defense + phillips + taxation + nationalization + redistribution + crime + welfare |
  south + midlands + north + wales + scotland + union + public + working_class + female + age +
  homeowner + income + education + inflation + taxes + unemployment
mb <- mnl(fb, data = bes1987, id = "id", alt = "party", ref = "alliance")
mb$loglik
#> [1] -1477.557
iia_tests(mb, seed = 1)
#> Tests of IIA / misspecification of the multinomial logit 
#>                                            test  alternative statistic df
#>                   Hausman-McFadden (difference) conservative    59.860 24
#>                   Hausman-McFadden (difference)       labour   -42.232 24
#>                   Hausman-McFadden (difference)     alliance   108.317 24
#>                        Hausman-McFadden (joint) conservative    25.395 24
#>                        Hausman-McFadden (joint)       labour    30.454 24
#>                        Hausman-McFadden (joint)     alliance    34.068 24
#>                Small-Hsiao (median over splits) conservative    21.212 24
#>                Small-Hsiao (median over splits)       labour    25.852 24
#>                Small-Hsiao (median over splits)     alliance    29.999 24
#>                 Fok-Paap CL Hausman (Q1, joint)                 67.563 41
#>  Fok-Paap GMM overidentification (Q2, two-step)                 44.544 31
#>   p.value   psd share_separated
#>  6.68e-05  TRUE              NA
#>   1.00000 FALSE              NA
#>  1.11e-12  TRUE              NA
#>   0.38455  TRUE              NA
#>   0.17015  TRUE              NA
#>   0.08347  TRUE              NA
#>   0.62620    NA               0
#>   0.36072    NA               0
#>   0.18479    NA               0
#>   0.00559  TRUE              NA
#>   0.05470    NA              NA
#> psd = FALSE: the covariance difference was not positive semi-definite for that row. A negative statistic is no evidence against the model (p-value 1); a positive one from a variance-difference form is unreliable (see the test's help).
#> Small-Hsiao (median over splits): descriptive, not a test at its level (it rejected in none of 300 samples in the package's size study); for the test, run one split with its seed fixed in advance (small_hsiao(m, seed = ), or iia_tests(m, splits = 1, seed = )).

The tests disagree, as they often do. The Hausman-McFadden test in its usual variance-difference form rejects for two alternatives. That form over-rejects, and its joint form does not confirm them: nothing in the joint form rejects at 0.05 (the Small-Hsiao medians are descriptive). (The difference form’s covariance difference is not positive semi-definite in a third row, which does not reject.) The composite-likelihood Hausman test of Fok and Paap rejects. The vignette Testing IIA and specification explains which forms to trust. A nested logit that puts Labour and the Alliance in one nest is a direct alternative:

mn <- nlogit(fb, data = bes1987, id = "id", alt = "party", ref = "alliance",
             nests = list(left = c("labour", "alliance"), right = "conservative"))
coef(mn)["lambda:left"]
#> lambda:left 
#>   0.8135637
lr_test(mb, mn)
#> Likelihood-ratio test
#>   LR = 4.4639 on 1 df, p = 0.03462

Its inclusive-value parameter, 0.81, lies inside the unit interval that random-utility maximization requires (the other two nestings of the three parties give values above 1), and the likelihood-ratio test prefers it to the multinomial logit at the 0.05 level: Labour and Alliance voters treat the two parties as closer substitutes than the multinomial logit allows.

Who leaves an insurgency: separation

defection holds the ex-combatants of Colombian guerrilla groups analysed by Oppenheim et al. (2015): were they captured, did they demobilize on their own, or did they switch to the paramilitaries? Oppenheim et al. interact the reasons for joining with what the group did, but the rare outcomes crossed with rare binary covariates leave empty cells: no captured combatant joined for economic reasons without being indoctrinated. Cook, Niehaus and Zuhlke (2018) show that the maximum-likelihood estimates of such interactions do not exist (a combination of the covariates predicts some outcomes perfectly: separation), and re-estimate the models with Firth’s penalized likelihood. Their penalized estimates of Models 3 to 5 reproduce.

data(defection)
with(defection, table(outcome, economic, indoctrination))
#> , , indoctrination = 0
#> 
#>              economic
#> outcome         0   1
#>   captured      4   0
#>   demobilized  35  13
#>   switched      7   2
#> 
#> , , indoctrination = 1
#> 
#>              economic
#> outcome         0   1
#>   captured     40   5
#>   demobilized 383  75
#>   switched     11   7
f3 <- outcome ~ economic * indoctrination + age_joined + birth_year + school_age + male
md <- suppressWarnings(mnl(f3, data = defection, ref = "captured"))
mf <- mnl(f3, data = defection, ref = "captured", firth = TRUE)
keep <- c("demobilized:economic", "demobilized:economic:indoctrination")
round(cbind(ML = coef(md)[keep], Firth = coef(mf)[keep]), 3)
#>                                           ML  Firth
#> demobilized:economic                 152.673  0.903
#> demobilized:economic:indoctrination -152.328 -0.632
separation(mf)
#> Quasi-complete separation: 15 of the 1164 comparisons the data report are separated, in 15 case(s);
#> the maximum-likelihood estimates do not exist.
#> Coefficients moving along some separating direction (the reported direction's coordinates):
#>                demobilized:economic demobilized:economic:indoctrination 
#>                                 0.5                                -0.5 
#>                   switched:economic    switched:economic:indoctrination 
#>                                 0.5                                -0.5

The maximum-likelihood fit warns that the data are separated (the warning is suppressed above), and its estimates are wherever the optimizer stopped. The penalized estimates are finite (Cook et al., Table 3: 0.903 and -0.632). separation() decides separation exactly, by a linear program on the comparisons the choices report, and names the coefficients along the separating direction: the economic-without-indoctrination contrast in both equations, since the empty cell is that of the base outcome, so raising both other outcomes there fits every one of its cases better. Under separation the Wald standard errors of those coefficients mean little; the profile penalized-likelihood intervals, the default of confint() for a penalized fit, and the penalized likelihood-ratio tests are the inference to use:

confint(mf, keep)
#>                                         2.5 %   97.5 %
#> demobilized:economic                -1.488544 5.828496
#> demobilized:economic:indoctrination -5.609336 1.969565
term_test(mf, type = "lr")
#> Joint tests of each term across equations (penalized likelihood ratio, Firth) 
#>                     term statistic df  p.value
#>                 economic     0.460  2 0.794707
#>           indoctrination    13.943  2 0.000938
#>               age_joined     6.162  2 0.045902
#>               birth_year     9.062  2 0.010769
#>               school_age     2.718  2 0.256971
#>                     male     6.204  2 0.044958
#>  economic:indoctrination     2.367  2 0.306274

The interaction that carried the published conditional hypothesis is far from significant once the penalty keeps it finite, as Cook et al. conclude. The penalty is invariant to the choice of base alternative, and it shrinks the fitted probabilities towards equal shares, so they no longer average to the observed shares. rologit() takes firth = TRUE too, with tied rankings.

Distance to the candidate, England 2010

bes2010 holds the respondents of the 2010 British Election Study in English constituencies, with the driving distance from each voter’s home to each party’s candidate (Arzheimer and Evans 2012). A party whose candidate’s distance is unknown is left out of the respondent’s choice set, so the choice sets vary: 234 respondents choose between two parties.

data(bes2010)
table(table(bes2010$id))
#> 
#>   2   3 
#> 234 440
mc <- mnl(chosen ~ feeling + incumbent + distance + deprivation | 1, data = bes2010, id = "id",
          alt = "party", ref = "labour", cluster = "constituency", se = "cluster")
summary(mc)
#> Conditional logit 
#> Call: mnl(formula = chosen ~ feeling + incumbent + distance + deprivation | 
#>     1, data = bes2010, id = "id", alt = "party", ref = "labour", 
#>     se = "cluster", cluster = "constituency")
#> Alternatives: labour, conservative, libdem  (base: labour)
#> 
#> Outcome equations (alternative:term):
#>                          Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)  
#> conservative:(Intercept)  0.33298    0.14278   2.332   0.0197 *
#> libdem:(Intercept)        0.05992    0.18450   0.325   0.7454  
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Generic coefficients (alternative-specific covariates):
#>               Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> feeling      0.8172822  0.0609151  13.417  < 2e-16 ***
#> incumbent    0.6457370  0.1566508   4.122 3.75e-05 ***
#> distance    -0.0060600  0.0024868  -2.437   0.0148 *  
#> deprivation  0.0003232  0.0115231   0.028   0.9776    
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Standard errors: cluster. Log-likelihood -328.472 on 6 parameters, 674 cases. AIC 668.94, BIC 696.02.

The same voters rated the parties after the election. Read as rankings, with equal ratings as ties, the ratings give a rank-ordered logit (the exact tie likelihood of Allison and Christakis 1994). A party the respondent did not rate is read as not on offer (its row is dropped), not as ranked below the rated parties:

r <- bes2010[!is.na(bes2010$rating), ]
r$rank <- stats::ave(-r$rating, r$id, FUN = function(v) match(v, sort(unique(v))))
keep <- stats::ave(r$rank, r$id, FUN = function(v) length(v) >= 2 & length(unique(v)) >= 2) == 1
mr <- rologit(rank ~ incumbent + distance + deprivation | 1, data = r[keep, ], id = "id",
              alt = "party", ref = "labour", cluster = "constituency", se = "cluster")
summary(mr)$coefficients
#>                               Estimate   Std. Error    z value     Pr(>|z|)
#> conservative:(Intercept)  0.5783995366 0.1184718597  4.8821681 1.049257e-06
#> libdem:(Intercept)        0.6097570718 0.0909177878  6.7066862 1.990938e-11
#> incumbent                 0.4494020525 0.1180507988  3.8068531 1.407463e-04
#> distance                 -0.0001369413 0.0007427007 -0.1843829 8.537131e-01
#> deprivation              -0.0079397433 0.0053962438 -1.4713463 1.411975e-01

Distance matters for the vote but not for the ratings.

Government formation in the German states

cabinets holds every potential cabinet at 125 government formations after German state elections (Baeck, Debus and Imre 2026): the authors’ potential cabinets of the parties in parliament, from 3 to 63 per formation. The alternatives are unlabelled (a cabinet at one formation is not the same alternative as at another), so the conditional logit has generic coefficients only and no alternative-specific constants (0 +); most potential cabinets never form, which such a model allows. The fit agrees with survival::clogit() on the same rows (the package’s test checks the log-likelihood to four decimals).

data(cabinets)
table(table(cabinets$election))
#> 
#>  3  7  8 15 31 63 
#>  1 21  1 38 44 20
mk <- mnl(chosen ~ 0 + incumbent + incumbent_newpm + minority + min_winning + bargaining +
            strongest + cross_cutting + het_economic + het_social + pea_res + rej_res | 1,
          data = cabinets, id = "election", alt = "cabinet")
summary(mk)
#> Conditional logit 
#> Call: mnl(formula = chosen ~ 0 + incumbent + incumbent_newpm + minority + 
#>     min_winning + bargaining + strongest + cross_cutting + het_economic + 
#>     het_social + pea_res + rej_res | 1, data = cabinets, id = "election", 
#>     alt = "cabinet")
#> Alternatives: afb, afd, cdu, cdu+afb, cdu+afd, cdu+dvu, cdu+dvu+ssw, cdu+fdp, ... (296 alternatives)  (base: afb)
#> 
#> Generic coefficients (alternative-specific covariates):
#>                 Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> incumbent         3.7724     0.6666   5.660 1.52e-08 ***
#> incumbent_newpm   2.5570     0.8423   3.036 0.002399 ** 
#> minority         -0.3939     0.9740  -0.404 0.685865    
#> min_winning       3.9542     0.8111   4.875 1.09e-06 ***
#> bargaining        2.0078     0.7941   2.528 0.011463 *  
#> strongest         2.1467     0.6396   3.356 0.000790 ***
#> cross_cutting    -0.7981     0.3386  -2.357 0.018416 *  
#> het_economic     -0.7999     0.1739  -4.599 4.25e-06 ***
#> het_social       -0.5306     0.1795  -2.955 0.003125 ** 
#> pea_res           3.8530     0.7348   5.244 1.57e-07 ***
#> rej_res          -6.4980     1.6873  -3.851 0.000118 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Standard errors: analytic. Log-likelihood -81.004 on 11 parameters, 125 cases. AIC 184.01, BIC 215.12.

pea_res and rej_res are the first-stage residuals of the authors’ two-stage residual inclusion (pre-electoral alliances and rejections), so their standard errors, like the published ones, ignore the first stage.

Leader attributes in Afghanistan

afghan_leaders holds the rankings of six attributes of political leaders by respondents of a survey experiment in three northern Afghan provinces (Bhatia and Monroe 2024), after one of four randomly assigned vignettes. Honesty and education lead, the mujahideen past trails, and the vignettes move the mean ranks little:

data(afghan_leaders)
round(tapply(afghan_leaders$rank, afghan_leaders[c("attribute", "treatment")], mean), 2)
#>             treatment
#> attribute    control bribery nepotism insecurity
#>   religious     3.06    3.24     3.14       3.11
#>   educated      2.26    2.14     2.23       2.22
#>   mujahideen    4.80    4.95     4.89       4.82
#>   government    4.15    4.10     4.06       4.15
#>   military      4.51    4.43     4.54       4.53
#>   honest        2.22    2.14     2.14       2.17
ma <- rologit(rank ~ 1 | treatment + female + age, data = afghan_leaders, id = "id",
              alt = "attribute", ref = "educated")
ma1 <- rologit(rank ~ 1 | treatment + female + age, data = afghan_leaders, id = "id",
               alt = "attribute", ref = "educated", depth = 1)
round(cbind(rankings = coef(ma), first_choices = coef(ma1))[grep("insecurity", names(coef(ma))), ], 3)
#>                                rankings first_choices
#> religious:treatmentinsecurity    -0.029        -0.248
#> mujahideen:treatmentinsecurity   -0.034        -0.052
#> government:treatmentinsecurity   -0.073         0.354
#> military:treatmentinsecurity     -0.064        -0.566
#> honest:treatmentinsecurity        0.013         0.116
rank_test(ma, after = 1)
#> Stability of preferences across ranking stages (position 1 against later; 2479 ranking(s) with later stages) 
#>              test statistic df p.value
#>  Likelihood ratio   401.151 30  <2e-16
#>              Wald   291.255 30  <2e-16

The rank-ordered logit uses the whole ranking, depth = 1 only the first choices. Their estimates differ, and rank_test() rejects equal coefficients for the first position and the later ones decisively: the respondents’ first choices follow other preferences than the rest of their rankings (or the respondents differ in ways the model does not capture; Allison and Christakis 1994). Then the pooled rankings are to be read with care, and the first choices alone are the conservative analysis.

References

Allison, P.D. and Christakis, N.A. (1994). Logit models for sets of ranked items. Sociological Methodology, 24, 199-228.

Arzheimer, K. and Evans, J. (2012). Geolocation and voting: Candidate-voter distance effects on party choice in the 2010 UK general election in England. Political Geography, 31, 301-310.

Baeck, H., Debus, M. and Imre, M. (2026). Incumbency advantages, prime minister replacements and government formation. Party Politics, 32(2), 183-196.

Bhatia, J. and Monroe, S.L. (2024). Insecurity and support for female leadership in conflict states: Evidence from Afghanistan. British Journal of Political Science, 54, 771-792.

Cook, S.J., Niehaus, J. and Zuhlke, S. (2018). A warning on separation in multinomial logistic models. Research & Politics, 5(2). doi:10.1177/2053168018769510.

Glasgow, G. (2001). Mixed logit models for multiparty elections. Political Analysis, 9, 116-136.

Liou, R.Y.-L. (2024). Mass mobilization, elite competition, and diversionary use of sanctions. Foreign Policy Analysis, 20(4), orae025.

Liu, R., Nagao, H., Hatungimana, W., Zhang, J.J. and Kennedy, J.J. (2024). The politics of flu vaccines: International collaboration and political partisanship. Japanese Journal of Political Science, 25, 61-74.

Oppenheim, B., Steele, A., Vargas, J.F. and Weintraub, M. (2015). True believers, deserters, and traitors: Who leaves insurgent groups and why. Journal of Conflict Resolution, 59(5), 794-823.
